rule: In king-and-pawn endings, identify the squares from which the king can force promotion regardless of opposition.

principle: Use the Rule of the Square Precisely
rule: Test whether a king can catch a passed pawn by entering its promotion square, then account for move order and interference.
In mutual zugzwang positions, identify pairs of squares where one king must answer the other's location.
Keep an unnecessary pawn move available when the position may become zugzwang.
Consider sacrificing one or two pawns when doing so forces a remaining pawn beyond the king's reach.
Use your king's opposition and body to deny the rival king the shortest route.
Recognize opposition even when three or five squares separate the kings on a file or rank.
Do not assume a knight can stop or support a rook pawn when the key squares lie at the board's edge.
With a rook pawn and bishop, compare the promotion square's color with the bishop's color.

principle: Use the Outside Passer as a Decoy
rule: Use a distant passer to pull the enemy king away from the main pawn mass.

principle: Use a Protected Passer as a Barrier
rule: A protected passed pawn can win by restricting the enemy king even before it advances.

principle: Respect Connected Passers on the Sixth
rule: Two connected pawns on the sixth rank can often defeat a rook when they protect their advance correctly.

principle: Give Rook Checks from Maximum Distance
rule: Keep checking distance so the enemy king cannot attack the rook while approaching.

principle: Use the Seventh Rank as an Endgame Base
rule: Place the rook on the opponent's second rank to attack pawns laterally and restrict the king.
Against a rook pawn and rook, check the king from the side before it can shelter behind the pawn.
Place the defending king on the short side of the pawn so the rook retains long-side checking distance.

principle: Cut the King Off Before Pushing
rule: Use the rook to exclude the enemy king by a file or rank before advancing the pawn.

principle: Verify the Pawn Ending Before Trading Rooks
rule: Calculate the resulting king-and-pawn ending to its conclusion before exchanging rooks.
In queen endings, improve the queen through checks that also approach central control.

principle: Control the Promotion Square in Queen versus Pawn
rule: Use checks to force the king in front of its pawn, then approach with your king while controlling promotion.
Before pushing a passed pawn, map the checks that could trap your king in a repeating zone.
Look for a checking move that interposes, attacks the enemy queen, or forces a queen exchange.

principle: Build the Fortress Around One Entry Point
rule: When materially worse, organize every piece around denying the opponent's only route of entry.

principle: Coordinate Bishop and Knight for Mate
rule: Drive the bare king toward the corner controlled by the bishop using a coordinated king, bishop, and knight net.
In a winning ending, neutralize checks, passed pawns, and active pieces before collecting material.
